result: The 3-D microsphere model recapitulates key cellular features of human tuberculosis granulomas. Cells initially distribute evenly within microspheres, then form aggregates by day 7 that are more numerous in infected versus uninfected microspheres. By day 14, large aggregates containing multinucleate giant cells similar to those in human TB patients develop. Monocytes mature into CD68+ macrophages, and T cell populations shift with increased CD4+ and decreased CD8+ cells over time.
evaluation: Claims C25-C37 collectively demonstrate that the microsphere model develops histological and cellular features characteristic of human TB granulomas, supported by microscopy (Figures 1A-J), flow cytometry (Figure 1D, 1H), and immunohistochemistry (Figure 1I-J). The comparison to human patient tissue (C34) strengthens the translational relevance. Statistical significance is shown for aggregate formation (C27).

result: The 3-D culture system significantly improves cell survival compared to 2-D culture and enables longitudinal analysis. Mtb-infected cells in 3-D collagen-alginate microspheres showed much greater survival than in 2-D culture as measured by LDH release and cytotoxicity assays. The system permitted analysis over 21 days, and decapsulation for downstream assays maintained >90% cell viability.
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C30, and C31 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F-G and Figure 1—figure supplement 4. The improved survival in 3-D is quantitatively demonstrated with appropriate assays (LDH, CytoTox-Glo), and the decapsulation procedure is validated. This addresses a key technical limitation of studying prolonged host-pathogen interactions.

result: Mtb proliferates within microspheres containing PBMCs and drives pathologically relevant host responses. In the presence of PBMCs, Mtb proliferates over 24 days reaching luminescence similar to broth culture, while growing slowly without cells. Infection upregulates matrix-degrading proteases (MMP-1, MMP-9) that functionally degrade collagen, and drives secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-12, GM-CSF, IP-10, MCP-1, IFN-γ) similar to those upregulated in human disease.
evaluation: Claims C38-C45 are supported by longitudinal luminescence data (Figure 2A), gene expression (Figure 2B, 2E), protein secretion (Figure 2C, 2F), and functional collagen degradation assays (Figure 2D). The multiparameter readout demonstrates both pathogen proliferation and host immune/matrix responses. The claim that cytokines are "similar to human disease" (C45) is interpretive but reasonable given the cited literature.

result: Extracellular matrix integrity, specifically type I collagen incorporation, favors host control over the pathogen. Collagen incorporation significantly reduced cell death and enhanced control of Mtb proliferation from day 7 onward, while elastin increased cell death. Collagen-containing microspheres showed increased apoptosis (a protective mechanism), altered cellular energy homeostasis (higher NADP/NADPH ratio), and increased secretion of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evaluation: Claims C46-C51 and C7 are well-supported by data in Figures 3B-K showing differential effects of matrix components on cell survival, bacterial growth, apoptosis, metabolism, and cytokine secretion. The conclusion that "matrix integrity favours the host" is justified by the reduced Mtb growth (C48, Figure 3C) and increased protective apoptosis (C49, Figure 3D) in collagen-containing spheres. Statistical significance is demonstrated throughout.

result: IFN-β and IFN-γ have divergent effects on Mtb growth and matrix degradation. IFN-β caused minor but significant suppression of Mtb growth and suppressed MMP-1 expression (suggesting a matrix-protective role), while IFN-γ consistently increased Mtb growth and increased MMP-1 expression. Both cytokines reduced cellular toxicity, and IFN-β further increased IFN-γ secretion, demonstrating complex cytokine cross-talk.
evaluation: Claims C52-C57 are supported by longitudinal growth data (Figures 4A-B), toxicity assays (Figures 4C-D), gene expression (Figure 4E), and cytokine measurements (Figure 4I). The divergent regulation of MMP-1 (C55) is directly shown, though the interpretation of IFN-β's "matrix-protective role" (C56) is inferential but reasonable. The unexpected finding that IFN-γ increases Mtb growth contradicts mouse model predictions but is consistent with cited human cell studies.

result: PGE2 augmentation suppresses Mtb growth but has potentially harmful effects on the host. Exogenous PGE2 suppressed Mtb growth in a dose-dependent manner, confirmed by both luminescence and colony counts. However, PGE2 increased secretion of pro-inflammatory IL-6 and neutrophil chemoattractant IL-8, suppressed IFN-γ secretion, increased cell toxicity, reduced cell viability, and suppressed apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C58-C64 are supported by comprehensive data in Figures 5A-H showing both beneficial (reduced Mtb growth) and potentially harmful effects (increased toxicity, altered cytokine profile, reduced apoptosis). The correlation between luminescence and CFU (C59, Figure 5B) validates the luminescence readout. This demonstrates the value of multiparameter analysis in evaluating host-directed therapies, though the clinical implications require further study.

result: Immunoaugmentation with Mtb-specific T cell lines paradoxically increases bacterial growth. ESAT-6 and CFP-10 specific T cell lines proliferated in infected but not uninfected microspheres, yet surprisingly led to increased Mtb growth compared to PBMCs alone. This was specific to antigen-specific T cells, as iNKT cell augmentation had no effect. Augmentation increased cytokine secretion (TNF-α, IL-1β) but did not affect cell toxicity.
evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by proliferation data (Figures 6B-C), growth curves (Figures 6D-E), and cytokine measurements (Figures 6F-G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The unexpected finding that antigen-specific T cells increase Mtb growth (C66) is counterintuitive but well-documented with appropriate controls (iNKT cells, C67). The authors acknowledge alternative explanations (ex vivo expansion artifacts) in the discussion, appropriately tempering the interpretation.

result: The bioelectrospray methodology was optimized for generating microspheres containing primary human cells and virulent Mtb. Ultrapure MVG-dominant alginate had optimal biophysical properties and minimal immunogenicity. Microspheres of 600 μm diameter were generated, cultured without media changes, and Mtb growth was monitored longitudinally by luminescence.
evaluation: Claims C81-C85 describe validated methodological details supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3 (alginate characterization) and the Materials and methods section. The alginate selection (C81) is data-driven, and the technical parameters are clearly specified. These methodological claims are well-supported and essential for reproducibility.

result: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is stated to kill more humans than any other infection, with 1.5 million deaths per year.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C11 present TB mortality statistics as factual assertions. While C11 cites supporting references (O'Garra et al., 2013; Horsburgh et al., 2015), C1 in the abstract does not. The claim that TB kills "more humans than any other infection" may be outdated or imprecise—HIV/AIDS and COVID-19 have at times exceeded TB mortality. The 1.5 million figure appears reasonable for the publication period but should be verified against WHO data.

result: The manuscript contextualizes the work within established knowledge about 3-D culture systems, TB pathogenesis, limitations of animal models, and emerging concepts in TB immunology.
evaluation: Claims C8-C24 and C70-C80 represent background knowledge and literature context, all supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the rationale for the study by highlighting: differences between 2-D and 3-D culture (C8-C10), TB pathogenesis features (C14-C15, C18-C20, C22-C24), limitations of mouse models (C16-C17, C71-C72), and emerging immunological concepts (C73-C80). The citations appear appropriate and the contextual claims are reasonable.

result: TB is characterized by spatially organized immune responses and extracellular matrix remodeling, and recent clinical trials and vaccine studies have been unsuccessful.
evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C6 describe established TB characteristics supported by the literature. Claims C12-C13 about unsuccessful trials are supported by citations (Tameris et al., 2013; Ndiaye et al., 2015; Warner and Mizrahi, 2014). Claims C14-C15 about the dual role of immunity are well-established in TB biology and appropriately cited. These contextual claims provide valid rationale for the study.
